topic: The Skin as an Organ, Primary & Secondary Lesions

cards.q: What is the integumentary system?
cards.a:
**The skin together with its accessory organs — hair, nails and glands.**

## Understanding it
- 'Integument' = covering; the system is the skin **plus** its appendages.
- Accessory organs: hair, nails, and glands (sebaceous + sweat).

>> Integumentary system = skin + hair + nails + glands.
opts: The skin, subcutaneous fat and muscle
The skin, mucous membranes and lymph nodes
The skin plus hair, nails and glands

cards.q: What does the word 'integument' mean?
cards.a:
**Covering — the skin is the outer covering of the body.**

## Understanding it
- 'Integument' literally means a **covering/coat**.

>> Integument = covering.

cards.q: Name the accessory organs of the skin.
cards.a:
**Hair, nails and glands.**

## Understanding it
- The skin's appendages are hair, nails, and glands (sebaceous and sweat).

>> Accessory organs: hair, nails, glands.

cards.q: Your lecturer says the skin is 'more than a simple body covering'. What three specialized components does she list?
cards.a:
**Glands that secrete fluids; nerves that carry impulses; and blood vessels that aid regulation of body temperature.**

## Understanding it
- The lecturer highlights glands, nerves and blood vessels as what makes skin 'more than a covering'.

>> Glands, nerves, blood vessels.

cards.q: Why is the skin often referred to as the largest body organ?
cards.a:
**Because it covers the entire body surface and serves as the main protective barrier for internal tissues.**

## Understanding it
- By surface area and mass, the skin is the body's largest organ, and its primary role is a protective barrier.

>> Largest organ: covers the whole surface, main protective barrier.
opts: It covers the whole body surface as the main protective barrier
It contains the most blood vessels of any organ
It weighs more than the liver and brain combined
It is the only organ with nerve endings

cards.q: Against what five things does the skin protect internal tissues?
cards.a:
**Trauma, ultraviolet light, temperature, toxins and bacteria.**

## Understanding it
- The barrier defends against physical (trauma), radiation (UV), thermal, chemical (toxins) and microbial (bacteria) threats.

>> Trauma, UV, temperature, toxins, bacteria.
opts: Trauma, UV light, temperature, toxins, bacteria
UV light, trauma, dehydration, cancer, ageing

cards.q: List the four functions of the skin.
cards.a:
**Protection, secretion, sensation and thermoregulation.**

## Understanding it
- Four core roles: barrier (protection), glandular output (secretion), sensory receptors (sensation), and temperature control.

>> Protection, secretion, sensation, thermoregulation.
opts: Barrier, vitamin D synthesis, sensation, storage

cards.q: As a protective membrane, what does the skin guard the deeper tissues against?
cards.a:
**Excessive loss of water, salts and heat; and invasion of pathogens and their toxins.**

## Understanding it
- As a barrier it works **both ways** — keeps water/salts/heat in, keeps pathogens/toxins out.

>> Prevents loss of water/salts/heat; blocks pathogens/toxins.
opts: Loss of water/salts/heat and invasion of pathogens/toxins
Loss of proteins and glucose only
Entry of UV light and cold only

cards.q: Name the two types of glands in the skin and their secretions.
cards.a:
**Sebaceous glands produce oily sebum; sweat glands produce watery sweat.**

## Understanding it
- Sebaceous → oily **sebum** (lubrication); sweat → watery **sweat** (cooling).

>> Sebaceous = sebum (oil); sweat = sweat (water).

cards.q: What is the function of sebum?
cards.a:
**It lubricates the surface of the skin.**

## Understanding it
- Sebum is an oily film that lubricates and helps waterproof the skin.

>> Sebum lubricates the skin.

cards.q: How does sweat help the body?
cards.a:
**It cools the body as it evaporates from the skin surface.**

## Understanding it
- Evaporation of sweat removes heat → cooling (thermoregulation).

>> Sweat cools by evaporation.

cards.q: What sensations do the nerve fibres under the skin act as receptors for?
cards.a:
**Pain, temperature, pressure and touch.**

## Understanding it
- Cutaneous receptors sense pain, temperature, pressure and touch.

>> Pain, temperature, pressure, touch.

cards.q: What is thermoregulation in the context of the skin?
cards.a:
**Several different tissues in the skin work together to maintain body temperature.**

## Understanding it
- Blood vessels (dilate/constrict), sweat glands and subcutaneous fat all contribute to temperature control.

>> Skin tissues jointly maintain body temperature.
opts: The epidermis alone insulates the body
Skin tissues cooperate to maintain body temperature

cards.q: Name the three layers of the skin from the outer surface inwards.
cards.a:
**Epidermis; dermis (corium); subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis).**

## Understanding it
- Outer → inner: epidermis → dermis → subcutaneous (hypodermis).

>> Epidermis → dermis → hypodermis.

cards.q: How does your lecturer describe the epidermis?
cards.a:
**A thin cellular membrane layer.**

## Understanding it
- The epidermis is the **thin, cellular** outermost layer (avascular).

>> Epidermis = thin cellular layer.

cards.q: How does your lecturer describe the dermis?
cards.a:
**A dense, fibrous connective-tissue layer.**

## Understanding it
- The dermis is the **dense fibrous** middle layer (collagen/elastin, vessels, appendages).

>> Dermis = dense fibrous connective tissue.

cards.q: How does your lecturer describe the subcutaneous tissue?
cards.a:
**A thick, fat-containing tissue.**

## Understanding it
- The hypodermis is the **thick, adipose (fat)** deepest layer — insulation and cushioning.

>> Subcutaneous = thick fatty layer.

cards.q: What is another name for the dermis?
cards.a:
**The corium.**

## Understanding it
- Dermis = corium.

>> Dermis = corium.

cards.q: What are the other names for the hypodermis?
cards.a:
**Subcutaneous tissue or subcutis.**

## Understanding it
- Hypodermis = subcutaneous tissue = subcutis.

>> Hypodermis = subcutis = subcutaneous tissue.

cards.q: In which direction do cells move within the epidermis, and what happens to them?
cards.a:
**Cells move from the base of the epidermis up to the surface, changing shape and structure (and dying) as they go.**

## Understanding it
- Keratinocytes are born at the basal layer and migrate **upward**, keratinising and dying by the surface.

>> Cells migrate base → surface, keratinise and die.
opts: From the dermis into the epidermis
From the base upward to the surface, dying as they go
From the surface downward to the base
They remain fixed and do not migrate

cards.q: Name the five layers of the epidermis from upper to lower.
cards.a:
**Stratum corneum; granular layer; spinous layer; basal layer; basement membrane.**

## Understanding it
- Top → bottom: corneum → granular → spinous → basal → basement membrane.

>> Corneum, granular, spinous, basal, basement membrane.
opts: Corneum, granular, spinous, basal, basement membrane

cards.q: What is the stratum corneum made of, and what is its role?
cards.a:
**Stratified squamous epithelium of hardened (dead, keratinised) cells that provide the skin's protective barrier.**

## Understanding it
- The outermost layer is dead, flattened, keratin-filled cells — the tough barrier.

>> Corneum = hardened dead keratinised cells (barrier).
opts: Hardened, dead keratinised cells forming the barrier

cards.q: Describe the granular layer.
cards.a:
**The transitional layer where keratinocytes develop into their final form and die; it contains keratohyalin and lamellar granules.**

## Understanding it
- Just below the corneum, cells here are **transitioning** — filling with granules and dying.

>> Granular layer = transitional, dying cells with granules.
opts: Transitional layer where keratinocytes finalise and die

cards.q: Which two granules are found in the granular layer?
cards.a:
**Keratohyalin and lamellar granules.**

## Understanding it
- The granular layer contains keratohyalin and lamellar (membrane-coating) granules.

>> Keratohyalin and lamellar granules.

cards.q: Describe the spinous layer.
cards.a:
**Keratin-producing epidermal cells forming a continuous net-like layer of protection for underlying tissue.**

## Understanding it
- The spinous layer's cells are linked by desmosomes ('spines'), producing keratin and giving strength.

>> Spinous layer = keratin-producing, net-like protective cells.
opts: Dead hardened cells at the surface
Keratin-producing cells forming a net-like protective layer

cards.q: What special cells are found in the basal layer?
cards.a:
**Melanocytes.**

## Understanding it
- The basal layer houses **melanocytes** (pigment cells) among the dividing keratinocytes.

>> Basal layer = melanocytes.

cards.q: What do melanocytes form and contain?
cards.a:
**A black pigment called melanin.**

## Understanding it
- Melanocytes make and hold **melanin**, which pigments the skin and absorbs UV.

>> Melanocytes contain melanin.

cards.q: Is the number of melanocytes different among the races?
cards.a:
**No — the number of melanocytes is the same in all races.**

## Understanding it
- Everyone has roughly the **same number** of melanocytes; only their activity/melanin output differs.

>> Melanocyte number is equal across races.
opts: Yes — it varies with sun exposure
Yes — lighter skin has more melanocytes
Yes — darker skin has more melanocytes
No — melanocyte number is the same in all races

cards.q: What accounts for the colour differences among the races?
cards.a:
**The amount of melanin produced, not the number of melanocytes.**

## Understanding it
- Skin colour depends on **how much melanin** each melanocyte makes, not how many there are.

>> Colour = amount of melanin, not number of melanocytes.
opts: The thickness of the stratum corneum
The amount of melanin, not the number of melanocytes

cards.q: What is the function of the basement membrane?
cards.a:
**It connects and functionally separates the epidermis and the dermis.**

## Understanding it
- The basement membrane anchors the epidermis to the dermis while keeping them distinct.

>> Basement membrane: joins yet separates epidermis and dermis.
opts: Connects yet separates the epidermis and dermis

cards.q: What three things does the epidermis NOT contain?
cards.a:
**Blood vessels, lymphatic vessels and connective tissue (elastic fibres, cartilage, fat).**

## Understanding it
- The epidermis is **avascular** — no blood/lymph vessels and no connective tissue.

>> Epidermis lacks blood vessels, lymphatics, connective tissue.
opts: Basal cells, spinous cells and corneocytes
Blood vessels, lymphatics and connective tissue

cards.q: How is the epidermis nourished?
cards.a:
**It depends on the deeper dermis and its rich capillary network for nourishment (by diffusion).**

## Understanding it
- Being avascular, the epidermis receives nutrients by **diffusion from dermal capillaries**.

>> Epidermis fed by diffusion from dermal capillaries.
opts: By diffusion from the dermis's capillary network

cards.q: What is the dermis composed of?
cards.a:
**Blood and lymph vessels and nerve fibres, plus the accessory organs of the skin.**

## Understanding it
- The dermis holds the vasculature, nerves, and appendages (follicles, glands) in a fibrous matrix.

>> Dermis = vessels, nerves, appendages in fibrous tissue.
opts: Blood/lymph vessels, nerves and skin appendages

cards.q: Which accessory organs of the skin are located in the dermis?
cards.a:
**The hair follicles, sweat glands and sebaceous glands.**

## Understanding it
- The skin's appendages sit within the **dermis** (some extend into the subcutis).

>> Dermal appendages: hair follicles, sweat glands, sebaceous glands.
opts: Hair follicles, sweat glands, sebaceous glands

cards.q: What is the main function of the dermis?
cards.a:
**To provide physical support and nutrients to the epidermis.**

## Understanding it
- The dermis mechanically supports and nourishes the overlying avascular epidermis.

>> Dermis supports and feeds the epidermis.
opts: Provides physical support and nutrients to the epidermis

cards.q: Name the two layers of the dermis.
cards.a:
**The papillary layer and the reticular layer.**

## Understanding it
- Dermis = superficial **papillary** + deeper **reticular** layers.

>> Papillary (upper) and reticular (lower).

cards.q: What does the papillary dermis contain?
cards.a:
**Smaller blood vessels that supply oxygen and nutrients to the lower epidermis, plus elastic fibres.**

## Understanding it
- The upper papillary dermis has fine capillaries feeding the epidermis.

>> Papillary dermis: small vessels feeding the epidermis.
opts: Small vessels supplying the lower epidermis, elastic fibres
Large vessels and dense collagen bundles

cards.q: What does the reticular dermis contain?
cards.a:
**Dense connective tissue, larger blood vessels, elastic fibres, and layered collagen bundles.**

## Understanding it
- The deeper reticular layer is the thick, strong, collagen-rich part with larger vessels.

>> Reticular dermis: dense collagen, large vessels, elastic fibres.
opts: Dense collagen, larger vessels and elastic fibres
Small capillaries feeding the epidermis only

cards.q: Which is the thicker layer of the dermis?
cards.a:
**The reticular dermis.**

## Understanding it
- The reticular layer is much thicker than the papillary layer.

>> Reticular > papillary in thickness.

cards.q: Name the five key cell types or structures within the reticular layer.
cards.a:
**Fibroblasts; mast cells; lymphatic vessels; epidermal appendages (rete pegs); and ground substance.**

## Understanding it
- The reticular dermis contains fibroblasts, mast cells, lymphatics, rete pegs, and ground substance.

>> Fibroblasts, mast cells, lymphatics, rete pegs, ground substance.
opts: Fibroblasts, mast cells, lymphatics, rete pegs, ground substance
Langerhans cells, Merkel cells, basal cells, sebum, sweat

cards.q: What is the role of fibroblasts?
cards.a:
**A key cell that repairs tissue damage (and produces collagen/scar).**

## Understanding it
- Fibroblasts synthesise collagen and drive wound repair and scarring.

>> Fibroblasts repair tissue (make collagen/scar).

cards.q: What is the role of mast cells in the dermis?
cards.a:
**They are involved in fighting infection (and drive allergic/inflammatory responses via histamine).**

## Understanding it
- Mast cells participate in defence and release histamine in allergy (producing wheals).

>> Mast cells: defence/allergy — release histamine.
opts: Involved in infection defence and allergy (histamine)

cards.q: What is the role of lymphatic vessels in the dermis?
cards.a:
**The lymphatic system is a key part of the body's defence against infection.**

## Understanding it
- Dermal lymphatics drain fluid and carry immune cells — part of infection defence.

>> Dermal lymphatics: immune defence/drainage.
opts: Part of the body's defence against infection

cards.q: What are rete pegs and what do they do?
cards.a:
**Epidermal appendages that interlock (link) the epidermis and dermis together to prevent shearing/skin damage.**

## Understanding it
- Rete pegs are downward epidermal projections that **anchor** the epidermis to the dermis, resisting shear.

>> Rete pegs interlock epidermis and dermis (resist shear).
opts: Interlock the epidermis and dermis to resist shearing

cards.q: What is ground substance?
cards.a:
**A gel-like substance that supports the cells within the dermis and provides structure.**

## Understanding it
- Ground substance is the amorphous gel matrix filling spaces between dermal fibres and cells.

>> Ground substance = gel matrix supporting dermal cells.
opts: A gel-like matrix supporting dermal cells
A layer of dead keratinised cells

cards.q: What is the subcutaneous layer composed of?
cards.a:
**Adipose (fat) tissue.**

## Understanding it
- The hypodermis is mainly fat — insulation and cushioning.

>> Subcutaneous layer = adipose tissue.

cards.q: State the two functions of the hypodermis.
cards.a:
**Protection of deeper tissues, and acting as a heat insulator.**

## Understanding it
- The fatty hypodermis cushions deep structures and insulates against heat loss.

>> Hypodermis: cushioning + heat insulation.
opts: Protects deeper tissues and insulates against heat loss

cards.q: Define a skin lesion.
cards.a:
**Any area of skin with characteristics (colour, shape, size, texture) different from the surrounding skin.**

## Understanding it
- A lesion is any localised change that differs from normal adjacent skin.

>> Skin lesion = an area differing from surrounding skin.
opts: A break in the epidermis only
An area differing in colour/shape/size from surrounding skin

cards.q: Give two examples of localized damage that produce skin lesions.
cards.a:
**Sunburns and contact dermatitis.**

## Understanding it
- Localised external insults (UV → sunburn; irritant/allergen → contact dermatitis) produce lesions.

>> Sunburn and contact dermatitis.

cards.q: Skin lesions can be manifestations of which underlying disorders?
cards.a:
**Underlying systemic disorders such as diabetes and infections.**

## Understanding it
- Skin can reflect internal disease (e.g. diabetes, infection).

>> Systemic disease (diabetes, infection) can show in the skin.
opts: Systemic disorders such as diabetes and infections

cards.q: How are skin lesions classified?
cards.a:
**Into primary lesions and secondary lesions.**

## Understanding it
- The core classification is primary (arising on healthy skin) vs secondary (evolving from a primary lesion).

>> Primary vs secondary lesions.

cards.q: Define a primary skin lesion.
cards.a:
**One that originates on previously healthy skin and is directly associated with a specific cause.**

## Understanding it
- Primary lesions arise **de novo** on normal skin from a specific cause.

>> Primary = arises on healthy skin from a specific cause.
opts: A lesion that has become infected
Arises on healthy skin, tied to a specific cause
Develops from another lesion by scratching

cards.q: List the examples of primary skin lesions your lecturer gives.
cards.a:
**Bullae, burrow, macule, nodule, papule, plaque, pustule, tumour, vesicle and wheal.**

## Understanding it
- Primary lesions include macule/papule/plaque/nodule/tumour (solid), vesicle/bulla/pustule (fluid), wheal, burrow.

>> Macule, papule, plaque, nodule, vesicle, bulla, pustule, wheal, burrow, tumour.
opts: Macule, papule, plaque, nodule, vesicle, bulla, pustule, wheal, burrow, tumour

cards.q: Define a secondary skin lesion.
cards.a:
**One that develops from the evolution of a primary lesion — through traumatic manipulation, treatment, or progression.**

## Understanding it
- Secondary lesions arise **from** a pre-existing primary lesion.

>> Secondary = evolves from a primary lesion.
opts: A lesion caused directly by sunlight
Develops from the evolution of a primary lesion

cards.q: Name the three ways a primary lesion becomes a secondary lesion.
cards.a:
**Traumatic manipulation (scratching/rubbing), treatment, and progression.**

## Understanding it
- A primary lesion evolves via manipulation, treatment, or natural progression.

>> Manipulation, treatment, progression.

cards.q: List the examples of secondary skin lesions your lecturer gives.
cards.a:
**Crusts, sores, ulcers and scars.**

## Understanding it
- Secondary lesions include crusts, sores/erosions, ulcers, scars (also scale, fissure, lichenification).

>> Crusts, sores, ulcers, scars.

cards.q: Define a vesicle.
cards.a:
**A raised lesion filled with clear fluid, less than 1 cm in diameter.**

## Understanding it
- Vesicle = small (<1 cm) raised **clear-fluid** blister.

>> Vesicle = clear fluid, raised, <1 cm.

cards.q: Define a bulla.
cards.a:
**A raised lesion filled with clear fluid, greater than 1 cm in diameter.**

## Understanding it
- Bulla = large (>1 cm) raised **clear-fluid** blister (a big vesicle).

>> Bulla = clear fluid, raised, >1 cm.

cards.q: What is the only difference between a vesicle and a bulla?
cards.a:
**Size — a vesicle is <1 cm, a bulla is >1 cm; both are raised and filled with clear fluid.**

## Understanding it
- They differ only in **size** (1 cm cut-off), not contents.

>> Vesicle vs bulla = size only (1 cm).
opts: Size only — vesicle <1 cm, bulla >1 cm

cards.q: Define a papule.
cards.a:
**A circumscribed, palpable elevation with distinct borders, less than 0.5 cm in diameter.**

## Understanding it
- Papule = small (<0.5 cm) **solid raised** lesion.

>> Papule = solid, raised, <0.5 cm.

cards.q: Define a plaque.
cards.a:
**An elevated area of skin with distinct borders and an epidermal change, greater than 1 cm in diameter.**

## Understanding it
- Plaque = large (>1 cm), flat-topped **raised plateau**, often with surface (epidermal) change (e.g. psoriasis).

>> Plaque = raised plateau, >1 cm, epidermal change.
opts: Raised plateau with distinct borders, >1 cm

cards.q: Which primary lesion uses a 0.5 cm cut-off rather than 1 cm?
cards.a:
**The papule.**

## Understanding it
- Most cut-offs are 1 cm, but the **papule** uses 0.5 cm.

>> Papule = the 0.5 cm exception.

cards.q: Define a macule.
cards.a:
**A circumscribed alteration in skin colour that is flat and not palpable.**

## Understanding it
- Macule = a **flat, non-palpable** colour change (e.g. a freckle).

>> Macule = flat colour change, cannot be felt.

cards.q: Define a patch.
cards.a:
**A large macule, greater than 1 cm in size.**

## Understanding it
- Patch = a macule >1 cm — still flat and non-palpable.

>> Patch = macule >1 cm (flat).
opts: A flat colour change >1 cm (large macule)

cards.q: Which two words in the definition of a macule tell you it cannot be felt?
cards.a:
**'Flat to the surface of the skin' and 'not palpable'.**

## Understanding it
- These two phrases confirm the macule is a pure colour change with no elevation.

>> 'Flat' and 'not palpable'.

cards.q: Define a nodule.
cards.a:
**A circumscribed, raised, solid lesion, ≤1 cm (deeper/firmer than a papule).**

## Understanding it
- Nodule = a solid raised lesion, similar size to a papule but extending deeper.

>> Nodule = solid raised lesion, ≤1 cm, deeper.
opts: A solid raised lesion, ≤1 cm (deeper than a papule)

cards.q: Define a wheal.
cards.a:
**A transient area of dermal (or dermal and hypodermal) oedema, compressible and usually evanescent.**

## Understanding it
- Wheal = a fleeting, compressible **oedema** swelling (urticaria/hives).

>> Wheal = transient compressible oedema.

cards.q: Which primary lesion is defined partly by TIME?
cards.a:
**The wheal — it is transient and usually evanescent.**

## Understanding it
- Uniquely, the wheal's definition includes its **short-lived** nature.

>> Wheal = the time-defined lesion (transient).

cards.q: What does 'evanescent' mean?
cards.a:
**That the lesion vanishes — it disappears, usually without leaving a mark.**

## Understanding it
- Evanescent = fleeting; it comes and goes.

>> Evanescent = vanishes/fleeting.

cards.q: Why is a wheal compressible?
cards.a:
**Because it is made of oedema fluid in the dermis, which can be pushed aside.**

## Understanding it
- Being fluid oedema (not solid), pressure displaces it.

>> Wheal is fluid oedema → compressible.
opts: It is dermal oedema fluid that can be displaced
It is filled with pus that drains
It is air trapped under the skin
It is solid tissue that flattens

cards.q: Define a burrow.
cards.a:
**A small linear tunnel in the skin that houses a parasite such as the scabies mite.**

## Understanding it
- Burrow = a thin, linear track dug by a parasite (Sarcoptes).

>> Burrow = linear parasite tunnel (scabies).
opts: A linear tunnel housing a parasite (scabies)
A pus-filled cavity in the dermis

cards.q: Which primary lesion's definition names its cause?
cards.a:
**The burrow — its definition states it houses a parasite.**

## Understanding it
- The burrow uniquely names its causal organism (a parasite) in its definition.

>> Burrow = the cause-defined lesion (parasite).

cards.q: Define a pustule.
cards.a:
**A circumscribed elevation of skin filled with pus, less than 1 cm.**

## Understanding it
- Pustule = small raised lesion filled with **pus** (not clear fluid).

>> Pustule = pus-filled, raised, <1 cm.

cards.q: What separates a vesicle from a pustule?
cards.a:
**The contents — a vesicle contains clear fluid, a pustule contains pus.**

## Understanding it
- Same shape/size range; the difference is **clear fluid vs pus**.

>> Vesicle = clear fluid; pustule = pus.
opts: Contents — vesicle clear fluid, pustule pus

cards.q: Define a crust.
cards.a:
**A hard, friable, irregular layer of dried blood, serum, pus or tissue debris adherent to the skin.**

## Understanding it
- Crust = dried exudate stuck on the surface (e.g. honey crust of impetigo).

>> Crust = dried exudate on the surface.
opts: Dried exudate (serum/pus/blood) adherent to the surface

cards.q: Define an ulcer.
cards.a:
**An open sore or erosion of the skin or mucous membrane (extending into the dermis).**

## Understanding it
- Ulcer = a full-thickness (into dermis) loss of surface → heals with a scar.

>> Ulcer = deep open sore (into dermis).
opts: An open sore extending into the dermis

cards.q: Define scaling.
cards.a:
**Whitish plates or flakes of stratum corneum present on the skin surface.**

## Understanding it
- Scale = visible flakes of the outer keratin layer (e.g. psoriasis, tinea).

>> Scaling = flakes of stratum corneum.
opts: Peeling of large sheets after injury (desquamation)
Whitish flakes of stratum corneum on the surface

cards.q: Define a scar.
cards.a:
**Fibrous tissue replacing normal tissue destroyed by injury or disease.**

## Understanding it
- Scar = collagen (fibrous) tissue laid down after dermal damage.

>> Scar = fibrous replacement of destroyed tissue.
opts: Fibrous tissue replacing tissue destroyed by injury

cards.q: Define erosion and oozing.
cards.a:
**Moist, circumscribed, slightly depressed areas — a blister base with the roof removed (epidermis only).**

## Understanding it
- Erosion = loss of **epidermis only** (the floor of a burst blister); heals **without a scar**.

>> Erosion = epidermis-only loss (no scar).
opts: Complete removal of epidermis by scratching (excoriation)
A moist blister base with the roof removed (epidermis only)
A linear crack down to the dermis (fissure)

cards.q: Define desquamation, and give the examples your lecturer gives.
cards.a:
**The peeling of sheets of scale after an acute skin injury — e.g. burns and toxic drug reactions.**

## Understanding it
- Desquamation = shedding of **large sheets** after acute injury (vs fine scaling).

>> Desquamation = sheet peeling after acute injury.
opts: Peeling of sheets of scale after acute injury (burns, drug reaction)

cards.q: Define excoriation, and give the example your lecturer gives.
cards.a:
**Oval-to-linear depressions with complete removal of the epidermis (from scratching), exposing the dermis.**

## Understanding it
- Excoriation = a **scratch mark** removing the epidermis; it tells you the lesion **itches**.

>> Excoriation = scratch-induced epidermal loss (itch marker).
opts: A linear crack to the dermis (fissure)
Epidermal loss from scratching (an itch marker)

cards.q: Define a fissure, and give the example your lecturer gives.
cards.a:
**Linear, wedge-shaped cracks in the epidermis extending down to the dermis, narrowing at the base — e.g. warts/hyperkeratosis at pressure sites.**

## Understanding it
- Fissure = a deep **linear crack** through the epidermis into the dermis.

>> Fissure = linear crack into the dermis.
opts: A linear crack extending into the dermis

cards.q: Define lichenification.
cards.a:
**Thickening of the epidermis (and somewhat the dermis) in response to prolonged rubbing.**

## Understanding it
- Lichenification = leathery **skin thickening** with exaggerated markings from chronic rubbing — a chronicity marker.

>> Lichenification = thickened skin from chronic rubbing.
opts: Skin thickening from prolonged rubbing (chronicity marker)
Peeling of sheets of scale after acute injury
A linear crack into the dermis

cards.q: Define gangrene.
cards.a:
**Death of tissue, usually due to loss of blood supply.**

## Understanding it
- Gangrene = necrosis from ischaemia (loss of blood flow).

>> Gangrene = tissue death from lost blood supply.
opts: Tissue death from loss of blood supply

cards.q: Which two secondary lesions are described as linear?
cards.a:
**Excoriation (oval-to-linear depressions) and fissure (linear cracks).**

## Understanding it
- Both excoriation and fissure have a **linear** shape.

>> Linear secondary lesions: excoriation and fissure.

cards.q: What is the difference between scaling and desquamation?
cards.a:
**Scaling is whitish flakes of stratum corneum on the surface; desquamation is peeling of large sheets of scale after acute injury.**

## Understanding it
- Scale = fine flakes; desquamation = sheets, after acute injury.

>> Fine flakes (scale) vs sheet peeling (desquamation).
opts: Scale = fine flakes; desquamation = sheet peeling after injury

cards.q: What is the difference between an erosion and an excoriation?
cards.a:
**An erosion is a blister base with the roof removed (spontaneous, epidermis lost); an excoriation is complete removal of the epidermis by scratching.**

## Understanding it
- Both lose epidermis, but excoriation is **scratch-induced** (linear) whereas erosion is the floor of a burst blister.

>> Erosion = burst-blister floor; excoriation = scratch mark.
opts: Erosion = blister base; excoriation = scratch-induced loss
Erosion is deeper than an ulcer

cards.q: Which secondary lesion tells you the lesion itches?
cards.a:
**Excoriation — it is produced by scratching.**

## Understanding it
- Scratch marks (excoriation) reveal the lesion is itchy.

>> Excoriation = the itch marker.

cards.q: Which secondary lesion tells you the process is chronic?
cards.a:
**Lichenification — it results from prolonged rubbing.**

## Understanding it
- Leathery thickening (lichenification) implies a **long-standing** process.

>> Lichenification = the chronicity marker.

cards.q: Which layer of the skin is important as a heat insulator?
cards.a:
**The subcutaneous layer / hypodermis, composed of adipose tissue.**

## Understanding it
- Fat conducts heat poorly, so the fatty hypodermis insulates.

>> Hypodermis (fat) = the heat insulator.

cards.q: Which layer contains no blood vessels?
cards.a:
**The epidermis.**

## Understanding it
- The epidermis is avascular, fed by diffusion from the dermis.

>> Epidermis = avascular.

cards.q: Which epidermal layer is the only one that contains melanocytes?
cards.a:
**The basal layer.**

## Understanding it
- Melanocytes reside in the basal (bottom) epidermal layer.

>> Basal layer = melanocytes.

cards.q: Which epidermal layer contains dead, hardened cells?
cards.a:
**The stratum corneum.**

## Understanding it
- The outermost corneum is dead, keratinised cells forming the barrier.

>> Stratum corneum = dead hardened cells.

cards.q: Which epidermal layer is described as the transitional layer where cells die?
cards.a:
**The granular layer.**

## Understanding it
- The granular layer is transitional — cells finalise keratinisation and die here.

>> Granular layer = transitional dying cells.

cards.q: Which layer of the dermis supplies the lower epidermis?
cards.a:
**The papillary dermis, through its smaller blood vessels.**

## Understanding it
- The upper (papillary) dermis's capillaries nourish the overlying epidermis.

>> Papillary dermis feeds the epidermis.

cards.q: OSPE — What is the golden rule when shown a photograph of a skin lesion?
cards.a:
**Describe before you diagnose — marks are awarded for accurate descriptive terminology even if the final diagnosis is wrong.**

## Understanding it
- In the OSPE, systematic description earns marks and leads to the diagnosis.

>> Describe first, then diagnose.

cards.q: OSPE — What is the first question to ask of any skin lesion?
cards.a:
**Is it flat or raised? If raised, what is inside — clear fluid, pus, solid tissue, or oedema?**

## Understanding it
- Flat vs raised (and, if raised, its contents) is the first branch point in classification.

>> First: flat or raised? then contents.
opts: How long has it been there?
Flat or raised — and if raised, what is inside

cards.q: OSPE — Give the ten-step sequence for describing a skin lesion.
cards.a:
**Type; flat/raised and contents; size; colour; shape and border; surface change; arrangement; distribution; and associated features.**

## Understanding it
- A structured description covers morphology, size, colour, border, surface, arrangement, distribution.

>> Type → contents → size → colour → shape/border → surface → arrangement → distribution.
opts: Type, contents, size, colour, border, surface, arrangement, distribution

cards.q: OSPE — Which size cut-offs must you quote when describing lesions?
cards.a:
**0.5 cm for the papule; 1 cm for vesicle/bulla, macule/patch, nodule and pustule.**

## Understanding it
- The papule uses 0.5 cm; the rest hinge on 1 cm.

>> Papule 0.5 cm; others 1 cm.
opts: 2 cm for nodules, 0.5 cm for the rest

cards.q: OSPE — What does a LINEAR arrangement of lesions suggest?
cards.a:
**Something external travelled or was applied along that line — a burrow (scabies), dermographism, or contact with an external agent.**

## Understanding it
- Linear = an **external** cause tracked along a line.

>> Linear arrangement = external cause along a line.
opts: An external agent travelled/was applied along a line
A random distribution with no meaning

cards.q: OSPE — You see a raised lesion but cannot palpate the photograph. How do you tell it is not a macule?
cards.a:
**Raised lesions cast a shadow and distort the surface light; a macule is a pure colour change with no shadow.**

## Understanding it
- On a photo you judge elevation by shadowing/light distortion — a macule shows none.

>> Raised lesions cast shadows; macules don't.
opts: You cannot tell from a photograph
Raised lesions cast a shadow; a macule shows none

cards.q: OSPE — A lesion is raised, well-demarcated, >1 cm, with silvery scale on the extensor surfaces. Name the lesion and likely diagnosis.
cards.a:
**The lesion is a plaque; the likely diagnosis is psoriasis.**

## Understanding it
- A well-demarcated scaly plaque on extensor surfaces is classic psoriasis.

>> Scaly extensor plaque = psoriasis.

cards.q: OSPE — You are shown a rash with macules, vesicles and crusts present simultaneously on the trunk and face. What is the diagnosis and what is the clinching feature?
cards.a:
**Chickenpox (varicella); the clinching feature is lesions at different stages of evolution present at the same time.**

## Understanding it
- Varicella shows all stages at once (macule→vesicle→crust).

>> Lesions at different stages together = chickenpox.
opts: Smallpox — all lesions at the same stage
Chickenpox — lesions at different stages simultaneously

cards.q: OSPE — How do you distinguish chickenpox from smallpox on lesion staging?
cards.a:
**In chickenpox lesions are at different stages simultaneously; in smallpox all lesions are at the same stage.**

## Understanding it
- Staging is the discriminator: varicella mixed, smallpox synchronous.

>> Chickenpox = mixed stages; smallpox = same stage.
opts: Chickenpox mixed stages; smallpox all same stage
Chickenpox all same stage; smallpox mixed

cards.q: OSPE — What is the single test that must never be omitted over a hypopigmented patch, and why?
cards.a:
**Test sensation with cotton wool (eyes closed), comparing with adjacent normal skin — an anaesthetic hypopigmented patch suggests leprosy.**

## Understanding it
- Loss of sensation over a pale patch points to tuberculoid leprosy.

>> Test sensation — an anaesthetic pale patch = leprosy.
opts: Test sensation — anaesthetic patch suggests leprosy
Test for fungal scale with a scraping

cards.q: OSPE — Give four differentials for a hypopigmented macule or patch in a child.
cards.a:
**Pityriasis alba; post-inflammatory hypopigmentation; vitiligo; pityriasis versicolor; and tuberculoid leprosy.**

## Understanding it
- Pale patches span post-inflammatory, fungal, autoimmune, infective causes.

>> Pityriasis alba, post-inflammatory, vitiligo, versicolor, leprosy.
opts: Pityriasis alba, post-inflammatory, vitiligo, versicolor, leprosy

cards.q: OSPE — How does vitiligo differ in appearance from pityriasis alba?
cards.a:
**Vitiligo is completely depigmented (chalk-white) with a sharp border; pityriasis alba is only partially hypopigmented with an indistinct, scaly border.**

## Understanding it
- Vitiligo total/sharp; pityriasis alba partial/fuzzy.

>> Vitiligo chalk-white/sharp; pityriasis alba partial/fuzzy.
opts: Vitiligo chalk-white, sharp border; pityriasis alba partial, indistinct
Pityriasis alba is chalk-white and sharp

cards.q: OSPE — You are shown raised, pink, linear coalescing lesions produced by stroking the skin minutes earlier. What is this?
cards.a:
**Wheals due to dermographism — a form of physical/inducible urticaria.**

## Understanding it
- Stroking triggers mast-cell histamine release → linear wheals.

>> Wheals from stroking = dermographism.

cards.q: OSPE — Describe the triple response of Lewis.
cards.a:
**Mechanical stimulation causes a red line (capillary dilatation), a flare (arteriolar dilatation), and a wheal (oedema) — via mast-cell histamine.**

## Understanding it
- Histamine produces red line → flare → wheal.

>> Triple response: red line, flare, wheal.

cards.q: OSPE — Which cell listed in the anatomy of the reticular dermis is responsible for producing a wheal?
cards.a:
**The mast cell — it degranulates and releases histamine.**

## Understanding it
- Mast-cell histamine causes the oedema of a wheal.

>> Mast cell → histamine → wheal.

cards.q: OSPE — A fine greyish wavy line 5 mm long with a dark speck at one end is seen in a finger web space. Identify it.
cards.a:
**A burrow — the dark speck is the female Sarcoptes scabiei mite at the advancing end (pathognomonic of scabies).**

## Understanding it
- The wavy line with a mite at the end is the classic scabies burrow.

>> Burrow with mite = scabies (pathognomonic).
opts: A scabies burrow (mite at the advancing end)

cards.q: OSPE — Where do you look for scabies burrows in an older child versus an infant?
cards.a:
**Older child: finger web spaces, flexor wrists, axillae, umbilicus, waistband, genitalia. Infants also: palms, soles, face and scalp.**

## Understanding it
- Older children spare the face; infants get palms/soles/face/scalp too.

>> Older: webs/wrists/axillae/waist/genitalia; infants also palms/soles/face/scalp.
opts: Older: webs, wrists, axillae, waist, genitalia; infants also palms/soles/face/scalp
Only the face in older children

cards.q: OSPE — Why is scabies itch classically worse at night?
cards.a:
**The skin warms under bedclothes, the mite becomes more active, and there are fewer daytime distractions.**

## Understanding it
- Warmth + mite activity + fewer distractions intensify night itch.

>> Warmth activates the mite → worse night itch.
opts: Histamine is only made at night
Cold air at night irritates the skin
Warmth activates the mite (fewer distractions at night)
The mite only feeds at midnight

cards.q: CLINICAL — Outline the treatment of scabies in a child.
cards.a:
**Permethrin 5% cream to the whole body from the neck down (including head/face, palms and soles in infants), left ~8–12 hours then washed off; repeat after 7 days and treat all contacts.**

## Understanding it
- Whole-body permethrin, repeated at 7 days, with contacts treated.

>> Permethrin 5% whole-body, repeat at 7 days, treat contacts.
opts: Permethrin 5% whole-body, repeat at 7 days, treat contacts

cards.q: CLINICAL — Why must scabies treatment be repeated after 7 days?
cards.a:
**The scabicide kills mites but eggs are more resistant; eggs hatch in 3–4 days, so the second application kills the newly hatched mites.**

## Understanding it
- Eggs survive the first dose; the repeat kills mites that hatch afterwards.

>> Repeat kills mites hatched from surviving eggs.
opts: Because the itch has not settled
Eggs survive the first dose; the repeat kills newly hatched mites
The first cream was too weak

cards.q: CLINICAL — Why must all household contacts be treated even if asymptomatic?
cards.a:
**An untreated contact is a reservoir; the child will be reinfested and treatment will appear to have failed.**

## Understanding it
- Contacts carry the mite silently and reinfect the child.

>> Untreated contacts reinfest — treat all together.
opts: It is a legal requirement only
They are a silent reservoir that reinfests the child

cards.q: CLINICAL — A parent returns saying the itch persists 2 weeks after permethrin. Has treatment failed?
cards.a:
**Not necessarily — post-scabetic itch is an allergic response to dead mite antigen and can persist for 2–4 weeks despite successful treatment.**

## Understanding it
- Ongoing itch after cure is an allergic echo, not failure (if no new burrows).

>> Post-scabetic itch ≠ failure.
opts: No — post-scabetic itch (allergy to dead mite) can last weeks

cards.q: CLINICAL — Why does secondary bacterial infection of scabies matter beyond the skin?
cards.a:
**Streptococcal skin infection is a recognised trigger for post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, so treating it protects the kidneys.**

## Understanding it
- Scratched, infected scabies can seed **strep**, which can cause **PSGN** (a renal complication).

>> Infected scabies → strep → post-strep glomerulonephritis.
opts: It causes rheumatic heart disease directly
Strep infection can trigger post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
It has no consequence beyond the skin

cards.q: CLINICAL — A 6-year-old has an itchy flexural rash with papules, excoriations and lichenification. What is the diagnosis and what does each secondary lesion tell you?
cards.a:
**Atopic dermatitis; the excoriations tell you it itches, and the lichenification tells you it is chronic (long-standing).**

## Understanding it
- Flexural itch + excoriation (itch) + lichenification (chronicity) = atopic dermatitis.

>> Atopic dermatitis: excoriation = itch, lichenification = chronic.

cards.q: CLINICAL — How does the distribution of atopic dermatitis change with age?
cards.a:
**In infants it affects the face and extensor surfaces; in older children it becomes flexural (antecubital and popliteal fossae).**

## Understanding it
- Infant eczema = face/extensors; older children = flexures.

>> Infants: face/extensors; older: flexures.
opts: Always only the palms and soles

cards.q: CLINICAL — Describe the itch–scratch cycle in atopic dermatitis.
cards.a:
**Itch leads to scratching, which excoriates and breaks the epidermal barrier, causing more irritation, more inflammation and more itch — a self-perpetuating loop.**

## Understanding it
- Scratching damages the barrier → more irritation/inflammation → more itch → more scratching.

>> Itch → scratch → barrier damage → more itch (a loop).
opts: The cycle is unrelated to the barrier
Itch → scratch → barrier damage → more irritation and itch

cards.q: CLINICAL — Using the anatomy of the skin, explain why emollients are first-line in atopic dermatitis.
cards.a:
**The defect is a failed stratum-corneum barrier that lets water out and irritants/allergens in; emollients restore the barrier, reducing water loss and irritation.**

## Understanding it
- Eczema is fundamentally a **barrier defect**; emollients rebuild it, so they are first-line.

>> Emollients restore the failed stratum-corneum barrier.
opts: They restore the failed stratum-corneum barrier

cards.q: CLINICAL — A febrile child has red macules. What single bedside test must you do and why?
cards.a:
**Press the lesion (or roll a glass over it); a non-blanching macule means blood outside the vessels — petechiae/purpura, suggesting meningococcaemia.**

## Understanding it
- The glass/pressure test distinguishes blanching erythema from **non-blanching** purpura (a red flag in a febrile child).

>> Do the glass/blanch test — non-blanching = purpura (meningococcaemia).
opts: Press/roll a glass over it — non-blanching = purpura (meningococcaemia)

cards.q: CLINICAL — Distinguish blanching from non-blanching red macules.
cards.a:
**Blanching means blood is still inside dilated vessels (erythema); non-blanching means blood has leaked out (petechiae/purpura).**

## Understanding it
- Blanches = intravascular (erythema); doesn't blanch = extravasated blood (purpura).

>> Blanching = erythema; non-blanching = purpura.

cards.q: CLINICAL — Give four causes of desquamation in a sick child.
cards.a:
**Burns; toxic drug reaction; scarlet fever; Kawasaki disease; staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome; and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.**

## Understanding it
- Sheet-peeling (desquamation) accompanies burns, drug reactions, scarlet fever, Kawasaki, SSSS, SJS.

>> Burns, drug reaction, scarlet fever, Kawasaki, SSSS, SJS.
opts: Scarlet fever, Kawasaki disease, SSSS, Stevens-Johnson syndrome

cards.q: CLINICAL — A child with sickle cell anaemia has a blackened, cold, dead toe. Name the lesion and explain the mechanism.
cards.a:
**Gangrene — death of tissue from loss of blood supply; sickled red cells cause vaso-occlusion, cutting off the blood supply to the toe.**

## Understanding it
- Sickling occludes vessels → ischaemia → tissue death (gangrene).

>> Gangrene from sickle vaso-occlusion (ischaemia).
opts: Gangrene — sickle vaso-occlusion cuts off blood supply

cards.q: CLINICAL — Why does an ulcer scar but an erosion does not?
cards.a:
**Scarring requires dermal damage; an erosion involves the epidermis only (heals without a scar), whereas an ulcer extends into the dermis.**

## Understanding it
- No dermal damage (erosion) → no scar; dermal damage (ulcer) → scar.

>> Ulcer reaches the dermis (scars); erosion is epidermal only (no scar).
opts: Ulcers damage the dermis (scar); erosions are epidermal only (no scar)
Scarring depends on infection, not depth

cards.q: CLINICAL — Which dermal cell is responsible for scar formation, and where does it live?
cards.a:
**The fibroblast, which lives in the reticular layer of the dermis.**

## Understanding it
- Fibroblasts in the reticular dermis lay down the collagen of a scar.

>> Fibroblast (reticular dermis) makes the scar.
opts: The melanocyte, in the basal layer
The mast cell, in the papillary dermis
The fibroblast, in the reticular dermis

cards.q: CLINICAL — Why is a preterm or malnourished child at high risk of hypothermia, in terms of skin anatomy?
cards.a:
**They have very little subcutaneous adipose tissue (the heat insulator) and a large surface area relative to body mass, so they lose heat rapidly.**

## Understanding it
- Little insulating fat + high surface-area-to-mass ratio = rapid heat loss.

>> Thin subcutaneous fat + high surface-area:mass → heat loss.
opts: Little insulating subcutaneous fat and a high surface-area-to-mass ratio
A thick stratum corneum blocks heat
Too much subcutaneous fat traps cold

cards.q: CLINICAL — Give three sterile causes of pustules.
cards.a:
**Acne; pustular psoriasis; and erythema toxicum neonatorum.**

## Understanding it
- Not all pustules are infected — acne, pustular psoriasis and ETN are **sterile**.

>> Sterile pustules: acne, pustular psoriasis, erythema toxicum neonatorum.
opts: Acne, pustular psoriasis, erythema toxicum neonatorum

cards.q: CLINICAL — Why should a well newborn with sterile pustules not automatically receive antibiotics?
cards.a:
**Erythema toxicum neonatorum produces sterile pustules in a well baby and resolves spontaneously — the pus does not mean infection.**

## Understanding it
- ETN is benign and self-limiting; pus here is sterile, so antibiotics aren't needed.

>> ETN = sterile, self-resolving pustules → no antibiotics.
opts: ETN gives sterile, self-resolving pustules in a well baby

cards.q: CLINICAL — Which primary lesion should prompt you to examine the lips, tongue, eyelids and airway?
cards.a:
**The wheal — the same histamine-driven process in deeper/airway tissue is angioedema, which can progress to anaphylaxis.**

## Understanding it
- Wheals (urticaria) can be accompanied by **angioedema** of lips/tongue/airway → check for airway compromise.

>> Wheal → check for angioedema/anaphylaxis (airway).

cards.q: CLINICAL — In which condition does the definition of the lesion itself give you the diagnosis?
cards.a:
**The burrow — its definition states it houses a parasite such as scabies, making it pathognomonic.**

## Understanding it
- Uniquely, defining a burrow already names the disease (scabies).

>> Burrow = pathognomonic of scabies (definition = diagnosis).

cards.q: CLINICAL — Why is erythema harder to appreciate in darkly pigmented skin, and what should you examine instead?
cards.a:
**Increased melanin masks the colour change; examine the palms, soles, conjunctivae and mucous membranes instead.**

## Understanding it
- Melanin hides redness on pigmented skin — look where pigment is lighter (palms, soles, conjunctivae, mucosae).

>> Melanin masks erythema → check palms/soles/conjunctivae/mucosae.
opts: Melanin masks it — examine palms, soles, conjunctivae, mucosae
It is easier in dark skin, no change needed
Use a Wood's lamp on the trunk

cards.q: CLINICAL — A child has honey-coloured crusts on the face. What is the likely diagnosis and which lesion type is the crust?
cards.a:
**Impetigo; the crust is a secondary lesion (dried serum, pus and debris adherent to inflamed skin).**

## Understanding it
- Honey-coloured crusts on the face = impetigo; the crust is a secondary lesion.

>> Honey crusts = impetigo; crust = secondary lesion.
opts: Psoriasis — the crust is a scale
Eczema — the crust is a wheal
Impetigo — the crust is a secondary lesion
Chickenpox — the crust is a primary lesion

cards.q: CLINICAL — Why can partial-thickness burns regenerate skin while full-thickness burns cannot?
cards.a:
**Epithelium regrows outwards from surviving hair follicles and sweat glands in the dermis; if the dermis (and its appendages) is destroyed (full-thickness), there is no source for regeneration.**

## Understanding it
- Skin regenerates from **dermal appendages**; full-thickness burns destroy them, so no regrowth (needs grafting).

>> Regrowth comes from dermal appendages — destroyed in full-thickness burns.
opts: Epithelium regrows from dermal appendages, destroyed in full-thickness burns
Full-thickness burns have too much melanin
